newsitem.title: BELGIUM: President says Bulgaria faces financial collapse.
newsitem.headline: President says Bulgaria faces financial collapse.

text.p: President Petar Stoyanov said on Wednesday that Bulgaria faced financial collapse and may have to default on its debt repayments to avoid a social explosion.

"Bulgaria is due to make payments on its external debt later this year which will face our financial system with a final collapse," he told NATO ambassadors in Brussels. "A default and a moratorium on our payments is not out of the question."

Appealing for Western help to overcome the economic crisis, Stoyanov said Bulgaria had not received proper recognition for its sacrifices in complying with international economic embargoes against former Yugoslavia and Iraq.

"I will be unfair to my fellow countrymen if I pass over in silence the fact of the just disappointment when the sacrifice Bulgaria made in the years of sanctions against former Yugoslavia remained on the sidelines of world attention," he said.
Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal who took office last week, laid much of the blame for the country's dire economic problems at the door of the ruling ex-communist Socialists.
But he added that the crisis had been increased by Bulgaria's loyalty to the international community over the sanctions on Yugoslavia.
"The universally recognised mistakes of the Socialist government were compounded by the fact of the billions worth of losses which Bulgaria suffered through the sanctions," he said.
He estimated the losses at half the country's total external debt of $10 billion.
In addition, he said, Bulgaria was owed $1.5 billion over the Iraq sanctions.
"We appeal for an urgent and adequate solution to this problem," he said.

Stoyanov, whose country has been shaken by 24 days of strikes and rallies, said "unpredictable social consequences" would follow if the economic crisis was worsened by meeting international debt obligations.
On his first visit to the West since taking office, he urged the European Union and NATO to support his country in its battle for stability.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said after the meeting it was not the alliance's place to solve economic problems. But he said he and the alliance's 16 ambassadors had listened with interest and sympathy and would transmit Stoyanov's message to NATO capitals.
Bulgaria is one of 10 eastern European countries to have applied for EU membership but is thought unlikely to be among the first group with which the bloc is expected to open talks next year.
Stoyanov said his country now also wanted NATO membership.

"Bulgaria does not want and sees no reason why it should continue to have a common border with NATO," he said. Later, he told reporters his election showed that the people supported his view because it had been a key part of his programme.
Organisations such as the International Monetary Fund have withheld credit to Bulgaria, saying the Socialists failed to embrace reform after their election in December 1994.
The IMF is withholding a $115 million credit. It says it wants to see action on closing loss-making state companies and privatisation.
After failing to find a compromise between warring political factions, Stoyanov on Tuesday asked Nikolai Dobrev, the interior minister of the Socialist party, to form a new government.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the mandate to the Socialists -- parliament's biggest party and the caretaker government since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
The Socialists rejected his call for them to return the mandate and agree to fresh elections.
